name: Socialmaxxing

lead: Socialmaxxing is the looksmaxxing-community term for improving social skills and social standing: making friends, joining circles and getting more comfortable talking to people. Its appearance payoff is that how attractive someone seems in practice depends heavily on how they carry themselves and who they are seen with.

Forum posters argue that a good social circle changes how others perceive you before you speak. Psychology research on social skills training and on the halo effect, where a positive impression in one area colours judgments in others, covers related ground, though it has not tested socialmaxxing as such.

paras: Forum guides describe taking the first step in approaching classmates or colleagues, greeting people, joining groups and clubs, and building a circle over time. Some threads pair it with style and status improvements.

There is little physical risk. Forum guides themselves note that the effort and initiative required fall on the person, and some posts discuss loneliness. People struggling with severe social anxiety or isolation may find professional support relevant.

angle.text: Posters say socialmaxxing raises perceived value through association and confidence, so the same face and body are received better. It works through how people react to you rather than by changing physical features.

lead: Socialmaxxing is a term from looksmaxxing forums for working on social skills, friendships and social standing. It sits alongside physical looksmaxxing: posters present it as a way to improve how a person is perceived and treated, including how attractive they seem to others [1][2].

One extended looksmax.org guide argues that membership of a good social circle sets someone's perceived value before they speak, citing acquaintances whose style and circle drew attention despite being short or having been bullied earlier [1]. Another thread aimed at users without friends advises taking the first step and not expecting friendship to arrive unprompted [2].

Outside the forums, social skills are defined as competencies that help people interact and communicate, and social skills training has research behind it in clinical settings [3]. Separately, the halo effect literature describes how impressions of attractiveness spill over into judgments of personality and social ability [4].

paras: Socialmaxxing covers conversation, approaching people, joining social groups and maintaining friendships. Threads on looksmax.org include guides to making friends at school, to networking and to going to college partly for social reasons [1][2].

A long guide on the forum claims the circle is among the most underrated variables in how people rank someone, saying it pre-qualifies a person by association [1]. Posters in another thread say school is an easy place to make friends by greeting people and offering compliments [5].
A guide for people with no friends frames the work as the person's own responsibility, saying nobody owes friendship and that most established groups will not approach outsiders [2].

Social skills are described as learned behaviours, and a 1985 meta-analysis of training methods found operant conditioning produced the largest effects, followed by modelling, coaching and cognitive techniques [3]. Poor peer relationships in childhood are linked to later difficulties, and training can help [3].

The halo effect, first named by Edward Thorndike in 1920, and the 1972 study by Dion, Berscheid and Walster found that attractive people were credited with more favourable traits including social skill [4]. Researchers also note that this stereotype can run both ways [4].
No studies found on socialmaxxing as such. Research on social skills training and on the attractiveness halo effect is described under research and expert views [3][4].

lore.intro: Socialmaxxing threads present friendship and social circles as part of the ascension toolkit [1][2].

claims.claim: A good social circle raises your perceived value before you speak.
Making friends takes initiative and is learnable.
